stem: A 9-year-old boy has a tender axillary lymph node 3 weeks after being scratched by a kitten. The biopsy shows stellate necrotizing granulomas, but no organisms are visible on the routine stain. A special stain is requested that shows small dark pleomorphic bacilli (see the picture).
oneliner: 9M + tender axillary node weeks after kitten scratch + stellate necrotizing granulomas + no organisms on H&E → which stain shows the bacilli?
ask: Which stain best demonstrates the organism?

whyNot.B: These small bacteria **stain poorly in tissue** by Gram stain, so it is not used to show them
whyNot.C: Stains **mycobacteria**; a **kitten scratch** with stellate necrotizing granulomas points to a different organism
whyNot.D: Highlights **fungi and glycogen**, not small bacilli
whyNot.E: Stains the **capsule of Cryptococcus** and mucin

answer: Warthin-Starry silver stain (Bartonella henselae)
why: **Cat-scratch disease** is caused by **Bartonella henselae**, a small pleomorphic Gram-negative rod. In tissue the bacilli are shown by **silver stains such as Warthin-Starry**. The node shows **stellate necrotizing granulomas** with neutrophils.

idea.rule: Tiny bacteria that Gram stain misses are found with silver stains.
also: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella in HIV): Warthin-Starry
Helicobacter pylori: silver stain or Giemsa
Legionella: silver stain (Dieterle)
Treponema pallidum in tissue: silver stain or immunostain

stem: A 19-year-old man has had burning on urination and thick yellow-green penile discharge for 3 days, starting after unprotected sex with a new partner. A Gram stain of the discharge is made, and culture grows oxidase-positive colonies on Thayer-Martin medium.
oneliner: 19M + purulent urethral discharge + dysuria + new partner + oxidase-positive growth on Thayer-Martin → Gram stain finding?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely seen in the discharge?

options.A: Gram-positive cocci in clusters seen in pus
options.B: Gram-negative coccobacilli lying in parallel chains
options.D: Clue cells with no neutrophils in the field
options.E: Many neutrophils with no organisms seen

whyNot.A: **Gram-positive clusters** (staphylococci) would not grow on **Thayer-Martin**, which suppresses gram-positive organisms
whyNot.B: **Parallel chains** are Haemophilus ducreyi, which causes a painful **genital ulcer**, not urethral pus
whyNot.D: **Clue cells without neutrophils** describe bacterial vaginosis in women; here there is **pus**
whyNot.E: **Neutrophils with no organisms** fit Chlamydia, but this isolate **grew on Thayer-Martin**, which selects for Neisseria

answer: Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils (Neisseria gonorrhoeae)
why: Oxidase-positive growth on **Thayer-Martin** with purulent urethritis identifies **Neisseria gonorrhoeae**. On Gram stain the organisms are **kidney-bean-shaped gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils**.

idea.rule: Gonorrhea = intracellular gram-negative diplococci in pus.
also: Neisseria meningitidis in CSF looks the same, but grows on blood and chocolate agar and ferments maltose
Cervical swab in women shows the same finding, though sensitivity is lower than in men
Chlamydia gives neutrophils but no organisms on Gram stain

stem: A 14-month-old unvaccinated boy has 2 days of fever, irritability and neck stiffness. CSF is cloudy with many neutrophils, and the isolate grows only when both hemin and NAD are supplied.
oneliner: 14-month-old boy + unvaccinated + fever + neck stiffness + cloudy neutrophilic CSF + growth needs hemin and NAD → CSF Gram stain?
ask: Which CSF Gram stain finding is most likely?

whyNot.B: **Lancet diplococci** are pneumococci, which grow on ordinary blood agar without **hemin or NAD**
whyNot.C: **Kidney-bean diplococci** are meningococci, which do not need **hemin and NAD** to grow
whyNot.D: **Gram-positive rods** suggest Listeria, a cause in newborns and older adults that grows on **blood agar**
whyNot.E: **Chains of cocci** are group B streptococci, mainly in **newborns**, and they grow on blood agar

answer: Small gram-negative coccobacilli (Haemophilus influenzae type b)
why: Growth that needs **factor X (hemin) and factor V (NAD)** on chocolate agar identifies **Haemophilus influenzae**, and the **unvaccinated** toddler points to type b. On Gram stain it is a **small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus**.

idea.rule: Haemophilus = tiny gram-negative coccobacillus needing X and V factors.
also: Satellite growth around Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar supplies factor V
Encapsulated, so the Hib conjugate vaccine targets the polyribitol phosphate capsule
Also causes epiglottitis in unvaccinated children

stem: A 45-year-old man has a crush injury to the leg in a farm accident, and the wound is soiled with dirt. Two days later the leg is swollen and crackles on palpation, the skin is bronze with blisters, and the wound smells foul. A Gram stain of the tissue shows few neutrophils.
oneliner: 45M + crushed leg 2 days ago + crepitus + bronze skin + foul odor + few neutrophils on smear → tissue Gram stain?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely in the wound tissue?

options.E: Large gram-positive rods with blunt ends

whyNot.A: **Clusters** (S. aureus) make pus rich in neutrophils; this smear has **few neutrophils** and the tissue has **gas**
whyNot.B: **Comma-shaped rods** (Vibrio vulnificus) infect wounds exposed to **seawater**, not a **dirt-soiled farm wound**
whyNot.C: **Branching filaments** (Actinomyces, Nocardia) cause **indolent** infection over weeks, not crepitus within **2 days**
whyNot.D: **Chains** (group A strep) cause fasciitis with many neutrophils and rarely **crepitus**; this smear has **few neutrophils**

answer: Large gram-positive rods with blunt (boxcar) ends and few neutrophils (Clostridium perfringens)
why: A **crush wound** contaminated with soil allows **Clostridium perfringens** to grow in dead muscle, making **gas (crepitus)**. Its **alpha toxin (lecithinase)** destroys cells and neutrophils, so the smear shows **large boxcar gram-positive rods with few neutrophils**.

idea.rule: Clostridial myonecrosis = boxcar gram-positive rods + gas + few neutrophils.
also: Alpha toxin is a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that causes a double zone of hemolysis on blood agar
Reverse CAMP test is positive
Treatment is surgical debridement with penicillin, not antibiotics alone

stem: A 49-year-old man who sorts mail at a large depot has 3 days of fever, cough and shortness of breath after a flu-like illness, and now confusion. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and CSF is bloody. A Gram stain of the CSF is done.
oneliner: 49M + mail sorter + fever + dyspnea + confusion + widened mediastinum + bloody CSF → CSF Gram stain?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely?

whyNot.A: **Small coccobacilli** suggest Haemophilus or Yersinia; neither gives a **widened mediastinum with bloody CSF** in a **mail worker**
whyNot.C: **Gram-negative diplococci** (meningococcus) cause meningitis with purulent, not **bloody**, CSF and no **mediastinal widening**
whyNot.D: **Lancet diplococci** (pneumococcus) cause lobar pneumonia and purulent CSF, not a **widened mediastinum**
whyNot.E: **Acid-fast bacilli** cause a **subacute** course; this patient deteriorated within days with **hemorrhagic** CSF

answer: Large gram-positive spore-forming rods in chains (Bacillus anthracis)
why: Inhaled spores reach mediastinal nodes and cause **hemorrhagic mediastinitis**, often with **hemorrhagic meningitis**. Bacillus anthracis is a **large gram-positive spore-forming rod seen in chains**.

idea.rule: Anthrax = large gram-positive spore-forming rods in chains (box-car), with a polypeptide capsule.
also: Edema factor is an adenylate cyclase; lethal factor is a protease
Protective antigen binds the host receptor to let the toxins in
Cutaneous anthrax gives a painless black eschar
Medusa-head colonies on agar

stem: A 32-year-old man camping in New Mexico develops fever, chills and a very tender swollen lymph node in the groin 4 days after flea bites near a prairie dog colony. Fluid aspirated from the node is Gram stained.
oneliner: 32M + New Mexico camping + flea bites + high fever + exquisitely tender inguinal node → aspirate Gram stain?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely in the aspirate?

options.B: Large gram-positive rods in long chains
options.E: Thin acid-fast rods in serpentine cords

whyNot.A: **Clusters** are S. aureus, which gives a local abscess, not a bubo after **prairie dog flea bites**
whyNot.B: **Gram-positive rods in chains** are Bacillus anthracis, spread by **spores or animal hides**, not **flea bites**
whyNot.C: **Diplococci** are Neisseria, which do not follow **flea bites** or cause a bubo with high fever
whyNot.E: **Acid-fast rods** cause a **chronic painless** node, not a **tender node with fever** 4 days after exposure

answer: Gram-negative rods (coccobacilli) with bipolar safety-pin staining (Yersinia pestis)
why: Rodent fleas transmit **Yersinia pestis**, which spreads to regional nodes and forms a **tender bubo** with fever. The aspirate shows **gram-negative coccobacilli with bipolar (safety-pin) staining**.

idea.rule: Plague = bipolar safety-pin gram-negative coccobacilli from a flea-borne bubo.
also: Southwestern US, prairie dogs and other rodents are the reservoir
Pneumonic plague spreads person to person by droplets
Tularemia is another cause of ulceroglandular disease, but with a small gram-negative coccobacillus needing cysteine

stem: An 8-year-old girl has fever and a very sore throat. Her tonsils are red with white exudate. A throat culture grows small colonies surrounded by a clear zone on blood agar, and a bacitracin disk inhibits their growth.
oneliner: 8F + fever + exudative pharyngitis + beta-hemolysis + bacitracin sensitive → Gram stain?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely on the isolate?

whyNot.A: **Clusters** are staphylococci; S. aureus is beta-hemolytic but **bacitracin resistant** and rarely causes pharyngitis
whyNot.B: **Lancet diplococci** (pneumococcus) are **alpha-hemolytic**, not beta-hemolytic with bacitracin sensitivity
whyNot.D: **Gram-negative diplococci** are Neisseria and do not produce **beta-hemolysis** on blood agar
whyNot.E: **Gram-positive rods** such as C. diphtheriae cause a **gray pseudomembrane**; beta-hemolysis with **bacitracin sensitivity** marks group A strep

answer: Gram-positive cocci in chains (Streptococcus pyogenes)
why: **Beta-hemolysis** with **bacitracin sensitivity** identifies **group A strep (Streptococcus pyogenes)**. Streptococci divide in one plane, so they form **gram-positive cocci in chains**.

idea.rule: Streptococci = gram-positive cocci in chains; staphylococci = clusters.
also: Group A strep is PYR positive and catalase negative
Group B strep is bacitracin resistant and hippurate positive
Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin sensitive and bile soluble

stem: A 3-day-old boy has fever, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle. CSF shows many neutrophils, and the Gram stain shows gram-negative rods.
oneliner: 3-day-old boy + fever + bulging fontanelle + neutrophilic CSF + gram-negative rods → organism?
ask: Which organism most likely caused the infection?

whyNot.A: Group B strep is a **gram-positive coccus in chains**, not a rod
whyNot.B: Listeria is a **gram-positive rod** with tumbling motility
whyNot.C: Meningococcus appears as **gram-negative diplococci**, and is uncommon in the **first week of life**
whyNot.D: Hib is a small pleomorphic coccobacillus that causes meningitis in **unvaccinated older infants**, not in the **first days of life**

answer: Escherichia coli (K1 capsule)
why: In the first month of life the main causes are **group B strep, E. coli and Listeria**. **Gram-negative rods** point to **E. coli**, usually with the **K1 capsule**.

idea.rule: Newborn meningitis: GBS = gram-positive cocci, Listeria = gram-positive rods, E. coli = gram-negative rods.
also: K1 capsule resembles the polysialic acid of neural tissue, helping it evade immunity
Listeria shows tumbling motility at room temperature
Empiric therapy covers all three organisms

stem: A researcher screens bacterial and fungal genomes for a gene that encodes an enzyme building lipid A, the anchor of lipopolysaccharide in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane.
oneliner: Experiment: gene for lipid A synthesis (LPS anchor in outer membrane) → which organism carries it?
ask: Which organism is most likely to carry this gene?

whyNot.A: **Gram-positive** with a thick peptidoglycan wall and **no outer membrane**, so no LPS
whyNot.C: A **gram-positive** spore-forming rod with **no outer membrane** and no lipid A
whyNot.D: Has **no cell wall at all** and a sterol-containing membrane, so no **LPS**
whyNot.E: A **fungus** whose wall is **chitin and glucan** with ergosterol; it has no lipid A

answer: Escherichia coli (a gram-negative bacterium)
why: **Lipid A** is the endotoxin part of **LPS**, found only in the **outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria**. **Gram-positive bacteria, Mycoplasma and fungi lack an outer membrane**, so only E. coli carries the gene.

idea.rule: Only gram-negative bacteria have an outer membrane with LPS (lipid A = endotoxin).
also: Lipid A binds TLR4/CD14 to cause fever and septic shock
The O antigen is the variable outer part of LPS
Gram-positive bacteria have teichoic and lipoteichoic acids instead

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a draining sinus along her jaw 6 weeks after a molar extraction. The pus contains small yellow granules that are crushed and stained for examination.
oneliner: 35F + draining jaw sinus 6 weeks after tooth extraction + yellow granules in pus → organism feature?
ask: Which feature identifies the causative organism?

options.A: Weakly acid-fast, aerobic, branching gram-positive rods
options.B: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles
options.C: Gram-negative rods growing under anaerobic conditions
options.E: Budding yeast with pseudohyphae in the sinus

whyNot.A: **Weakly acid-fast aerobic rods** are Nocardia, a cause of **lung and brain** infection in immunocompromised patients, not jaw sinuses
whyNot.B: **Acute-angle septate hyphae** are Aspergillus, seen in **neutropenic** patients, not **yellow granules** in a jaw sinus
whyNot.C: **Gram-negative rods** do not form **yellow (sulfur) granules** in a sinus after dental work
whyNot.E: **Pseudohyphae** are Candida, which causes **thrush**, not a draining sinus with **yellow granules**

answer: Gram-positive, branching, anaerobic, non-acid-fast filaments (Actinomyces israelii)
why: A **draining jaw sinus** after **dental work** with **yellow sulfur granules** is **cervicofacial actinomycosis**. Actinomyces israelii is a **gram-positive anaerobic branching filament** that is **not acid-fast**, unlike Nocardia.

idea.rule: Actinomyces = anaerobic, not acid-fast; Nocardia = aerobic, weakly acid-fast.
also: Actinomyces is normal oral flora; disease follows trauma or dental work
Treated with prolonged penicillin
Nocardia causes pulmonary and brain abscesses in immunocompromised patients
Sulfur granules are bacterial colonies, not sulfur

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a central venous catheter and parenteral nutrition after bowel surgery. She remains febrile for 5 days despite vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam. A blood culture bottle turns positive and is Gram stained.
oneliner: 70F + central line + TPN after surgery + fever despite vancomycin and pip-tazo → blood culture Gram stain?
ask: Which Gram stain finding is most likely in the blood culture?

options.C: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles

whyNot.B: **Clusters** (staphylococci) would be killed by **vancomycin**, which she is already receiving
whyNot.C: **Septate acute-angle hyphae** (Aspergillus) are rarely seen in **blood cultures**, and the risk factors differ
whyNot.D: **Narrow-based budding with a capsule** is Cryptococcus, causing **meningitis** in HIV, not a line infection with TPN
whyNot.E: **Gram-negative rods** are covered by **piperacillin-tazobactam**, which she is already receiving

answer: Oval gram-positive budding yeast, about 4 microns (Candida)
why: A **central line**, **TPN** and **fever despite broad antibiotics** point to **candidemia**. Candida is an **oval budding yeast that stains gram-positive (purple)**, about 4 microns across.

idea.rule: Fever despite antibacterials + line or TPN = Candida; yeasts stain gram-positive.
also: Candida albicans forms germ tubes at 37 C
Echinocandins are first-line for candidemia
Remove the central line
Candida is also seen as pseudohyphae in tissue

stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes presents in ketoacidosis with facial pain and swelling. He has a black, dead area of tissue on his palate, and a biopsy of the area is examined.
oneliner: 52M + diabetic ketoacidosis + facial pain + black necrotic palate eschar → biopsy finding?
ask: Which finding is most likely seen on the biopsy?

options.A: Narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles
options.B: Yeast with a single broad-based bud
options.C: Broad nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles

whyNot.A: **Acute-angle septate hyphae** are Aspergillus, which does not typically cause this **ketoacidosis-linked** palate necrosis
whyNot.B: **Broad-based budding** is Blastomyces, which causes **pneumonia and skin lesions**, not black palate eschar
whyNot.D: **Pseudohyphae with yeast** are Candida, causing superficial or mucosal **thrush**, not tissue-**invasive black necrosis**
whyNot.E: **Spherules with endospores** are Coccidioides, from **southwestern desert exposure**, which does not cause this picture

answer: Broad, ribbon-like nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching (Mucorales)
why: **Ketoacidosis** with a **black necrotic palate or nasal eschar** is **rhinocerebral mucormycosis** from Mucor or Rhizopus. Biopsy shows **broad nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles**.

idea.rule: Mucormycosis = ketoacidosis + black eschar + broad nonseptate right-angle hyphae.
also: Invades blood vessels, causing infarction and black necrosis
Treated with amphotericin B and surgical debridement
Also a risk in neutropenia and deferoxamine therapy
Aspergillus has septate hyphae at 45 degrees

stem: A 40-year-old previously healthy man from Wisconsin develops cough, fever and chest pain two months after a canoe trip. He now has several raised, wart-like skin lesions on his arm. A skin biopsy is examined.
oneliner: 40M + healthy + Wisconsin canoe trip + pneumonia + verrucous skin lesions → biopsy form?
ask: Which tissue form is most likely seen in the biopsy?

options.D: Yeast with multiple buds like a ship's wheel
options.E: Thick-walled yeast with one broad-based bud

whyNot.A: **Narrow-based buds with a capsule** are Cryptococcus, which mainly causes **meningitis** in immunocompromised patients, not a **healthy** man
whyNot.B: **Spherules** are Coccidioides, from the **southwestern desert**, not the upper Midwest
whyNot.C: **Small intracellular yeast** are Histoplasma, which rarely causes **wart-like skin lesions**
whyNot.D: **Ship's wheel** budding is Paracoccidioides, found in **Latin America**

answer: Thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding (Blastomyces dermatitidis)
why: **Pneumonia plus verrucous skin lesions** after exposure to **soil near water in the Great Lakes region** suggests **blastomycosis**. The tissue form is a **thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding**.

idea.rule: Blastomyces = broad-based budding; Cryptococcus = narrow-based budding.
also: Endemic in the Great Lakes, Ohio and Mississippi river regions
Treated with itraconazole, or amphotericin B if severe
Dimorphic: mold at 25 C, yeast at 37 C

stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 50 has had headache and fever for 2 weeks. His opening pressure at lumbar puncture is elevated, and an India ink preparation of the CSF is examined.
oneliner: 38M + AIDS (CD4 50) + 2 weeks of headache and fever + high opening pressure → CSF finding?
ask: Which CSF finding is most likely seen?

options.A: Yeast with a single broad-based bud
options.B: Budding yeast with a clear halo
options.C: Narrow septate hyphae at acute angles

whyNot.A: **Broad-based budding** is Blastomyces, which rarely causes meningitis and does not give a **halo on India ink**
whyNot.C: **Septate hyphae** are Aspergillus, which seldom infects CSF and does not give a **subacute high-pressure** picture with a halo
whyNot.D: **Gram-positive rods** (Listeria) cause **acute** meningitis, not a **2-week course with raised pressure**
whyNot.E: **Pseudohyphae** are Candida, which causes thrush or line infections rather than **high-pressure meningitis**

answer: Encapsulated budding yeast with a clear halo on India ink (Cryptococcus neoformans)
why: **Subacute meningitis**, **high opening pressure** and **CD4 below 100** suggest **cryptococcal meningitis**. The thick polysaccharide capsule excludes India ink, giving a **clear halo around budding yeast**.

idea.rule: Cryptococcus = capsule halo on India ink, narrow-based budding.
also: Mucicarmine stains the capsule deep red
Latex agglutination detects capsular antigen in CSF
Associated with pigeon droppings
Treat with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole

stem: A 22-year-old man notices pale, slightly scaly patches on his upper back and chest after a humid summer. They do not itch. Skin scrapings are treated with potassium hydroxide and examined.
oneliner: 22M + hypopigmented scaly macules on upper back after a humid summer + KOH prep → finding?
ask: Which KOH preparation finding is most likely?

whyNot.A: **Hyphae only** are dermatophytes (tinea corporis), which form **itchy annular plaques with a scaly edge**
whyNot.B: **Giant cells** (Tzanck) suggest herpesvirus infection with **painful vesicles**
whyNot.C: **Pseudohyphae with yeast** are Candida, giving **red, moist** lesions in skin folds
whyNot.E: **Broad nonseptate hyphae** are Mucor, seen in **ketoacidotic or neutropenic** patients, not in a well man with scaly macules

answer: Short hyphae with round yeast, spaghetti and meatballs (Malassezia)
why: **Pale scaly macules** that appear in **hot, humid weather** are **tinea versicolor** from **Malassezia**. A KOH prep shows **short hyphae with clustered round yeast** (spaghetti and meatballs).

idea.rule: Tinea versicolor = spaghetti-and-meatballs on KOH; dermatophytes = hyphae only.
also: Malassezia is lipophilic and digests skin lipids, so it blocks pigment production
Treat with topical selenium sulfide or azoles
Malassezia furfur can cause line sepsis with lipid infusions

stem: A 45-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 2 months ago has fever, dry cough and breathlessness. Chest imaging shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and a blood PCR for CMV DNA is strongly positive. A lung biopsy is examined.
oneliner: 45M + kidney transplant 2 months ago + fever, cough, diffuse infiltrates + positive CMV PCR → lung biopsy finding?
ask: Which biopsy finding is most likely seen?

options.E: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles

whyNot.B: **Giant cells without inclusions** suggest measles or RSV pneumonia, but this patient has a **positive CMV PCR**
whyNot.C: **Smudge cells** are adenovirus, whose pneumonia does not fit **transplant with a positive CMV PCR**
whyNot.D: **Negri bodies** are rabies, which affects the **nervous system**, not the lung
whyNot.E: **Septate hyphae** mean Aspergillus, but the **CMV PCR is positive** and the infiltrates are diffuse rather than nodular

answer: Enlarged cell with a large intranuclear owl's eye inclusion (CMV)
why: **Immunosuppression after transplant** with **pneumonitis** and **positive CMV PCR** means **CMV pneumonitis**. Infected cells are **enlarged (cytomegaly)** with a **large basophilic intranuclear inclusion** surrounded by a halo, the owl's eye.

idea.rule: CMV = cytomegaly + owl's eye intranuclear inclusion.
also: Treated with ganciclovir; foscarnet if resistant
CMV also causes retinitis in AIDS and colitis in transplant recipients
Congenital CMV gives periventricular calcifications and deafness

stem: A 10-day-old girl delivered vaginally has had three days of watery, then thick yellow discharge from both eyes, with puffy eyelids. Her mother had no prenatal care and was never screened for genital infections. Conjunctival scrapings are stained with Giemsa.
oneliner: 10-day-old F + bilateral watery then mucopurulent eye discharge from day 7 + swollen lids + unscreened mother + Giemsa of scrapings → which finding?
ask: Which finding on the stained scraping is most likely?

options.B: Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions
options.D: Large cells with a central intranuclear 'owl's eye' inclusion

whyNot.A: **Gonococcal** conjunctivitis begins within **2 to 5 days** of birth and is hyperpurulent from the start; her discharge began at **1 week** and was **watery first**
whyNot.B: **HSV** disease shows **vesicles** or corneal dendrites; she has **no vesicles**, only discharge and lid swelling
whyNot.D: **CMV** is a congenital infection with systemic signs; this infant has **isolated conjunctivitis** that began after the first days of life
whyNot.E: **S. aureus** conjunctivitis is not linked to an **unscreened mother's genital infection**, and clusters of cocci are not an **inclusion** finding in scraped epithelial cells

answer: Intracytoplasmic basophilic inclusion bodies (Chlamydia trachomatis)
why: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism, so Giemsa of conjunctival scrapings shows **cytoplasmic inclusions in epithelial cells**. Onset at about **5 to 14 days** after birth from an **untreated mother** fits chlamydial, not gonococcal, conjunctivitis.

idea.rule: Obligate intracellular organisms are found as inclusions or in host cells, not on a Gram stain.
also: Chlamydia: cytoplasmic inclusions (Giemsa) in epithelial cells
Rickettsia: Giemsa or Gimenez shows organisms in endothelial cells
Ehrlichia and Anaplasma: morulae inside leukocytes
CMV: intranuclear owl's-eye inclusions

stem: A 10-year-old boy living in a mud-walled house in rural Bolivia has had fever for 4 days and a painless, firm swelling of the left eyelid and cheek that began after an insect bite near that eye. A thick blood smear is examined.
oneliner: 10M + rural Bolivia mud house + fever + painless unilateral eyelid swelling after bug bite + blood smear → which finding?
ask: Which blood smear finding is most likely?

options.A: C-shaped flagellated forms among red cells
options.B: Small ring-shaped parasites inside red blood cells
options.C: Tetrads shaped like Maltese crosses inside red cells
options.E: Round non-flagellated forms packed inside macrophages

whyNot.B: **Malaria** causes cyclic fever, not a **painless unilateral eyelid swelling** after a bug bite
whyNot.C: **Babesia** follows a **tick** bite and causes hemolysis; this boy was bitten by a **flying insect near the eye**
whyNot.D: **P. falciparum gametocytes** mean malaria, which does not cause a **painless swollen eyelid at a bite** near the eye
whyNot.E: **Leishmania amastigotes** sit inside macrophages of spleen, liver or skin after a **sandfly** bite; they do not explain **painless eyelid swelling** at a bite by the eye

answer: Trypomastigotes in the blood (Trypanosoma cruzi)
why: A unilateral painless eyelid swelling after a **triatomine bite** is the **Romana sign** of acute Chagas disease. In the acute phase the blood smear shows **C-shaped trypomastigotes**; amastigotes live in tissue (heart, gut), not free in the blood.

idea.rule: Acute Chagas is diagnosed by seeing the parasite in blood; chronic Chagas is diagnosed by serology.
also: Acute Chagas: C-shaped trypomastigotes on a blood smear
Chronic Chagas: serology, because blood parasites are scant
Chronic disease: amastigotes in heart and gut muscle (myocarditis, megaesophagus, megacolon)
African trypanosomiasis: trypomastigotes in blood, lymph node aspirate or CSF

stem: A 30-year-old man returned from a month in sub-Saharan Africa without taking prophylaxis. He now has a temperature of 40.1 C, confusion and pallor, with hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL. He recalls no tick bites. Thick and thin blood smears are examined.
oneliner: 30M + back from sub-Saharan Africa, no prophylaxis + fever 40.1 + confusion + Hb 7.4 + no tick bite → which smear finding?
ask: Which blood smear finding is most likely?

options.A: Tetrads shaped like Maltese crosses inside red cells
options.B: Enlarged red cells containing Schuffner stippling and ameboid rings
options.C: Large loosely coiled spirochetes between red cells
options.E: Small ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes in red cells

whyNot.A: **Babesia** needs a **tick** exposure in an endemic region; he recalls **no tick bites** and has a month of African travel
whyNot.B: These are **vivax or ovale** features; they infect young cells and rarely cause **confusion with severe anemia and a high fever**
whyNot.C: **Relapsing fever** needs a tick or louse exposure and produces **febrile episodes separated by well intervals**; he has no tick bites
whyNot.D: **Ehrlichia morulae** follow a **tick bite** in the United States; he reports none and has traveled to Africa

answer: Ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes (Plasmodium falciparum)
why: **Travel to Africa** with high fever, **confusion** and anemia suggests severe falciparum malaria. P. falciparum infects red cells of all ages, so smears show **multiple small rings** and the characteristic **banana-shaped gametocytes**.

idea.rule: Banana-shaped gametocytes = falciparum; Schuffner stippling and enlarged cells = vivax or ovale.
also: P. falciparum infects red cells of all ages and causes the highest parasitemia
P. vivax and ovale infect young red cells and show Schuffner stippling
P. malariae infects old red cells and shows band forms
Babesia: ring forms and Maltese cross tetrads after an Ixodes bite

stem: A 25-year-old man has had three episodes of fever and headache, each lasting about 3 days and separated by roughly a week of feeling well, since sleeping in a rodent-infested mountain cabin. A Giemsa-stained blood smear is taken while he is febrile.
oneliner: 25M + three 3-day fever bouts a week apart + rodent-infested mountain cabin + Giemsa smear during fever → which finding?
ask: Which blood smear finding is most likely?

options.A: Small ring-shaped parasites inside red blood cells
options.B: Large coiled spirochetes between red cells
options.C: Tetrads shaped like Maltese crosses inside red cells
options.E: C-shaped flagellated forms among the red cells

whyNot.A: **Malaria** fevers recur every **48 to 72 hours**, not as **3-day bouts separated by about a week** of feeling well
whyNot.C: **Babesia** causes persistent hemolytic fever, not **repeated febrile bouts with long well intervals** after a rodent cabin stay
whyNot.D: **Ehrlichia morulae** cause one continuous febrile illness with low counts, not **relapses separated by a week of health**
whyNot.E: **Trypomastigotes** of acute Chagas give one continuing febrile illness after a reduviid bite, not **relapses a week apart**

answer: Borrelia spirochetes on blood smear (relapsing fever)
why: **Recurrent fever** after a rodent-infested cabin stay suggests tick-borne relapsing fever. Borrelia are large enough to be seen on **Giemsa or Wright smears** taken during fever; relapses occur because **antigenic variation** escapes antibodies.

idea.rule: Borrelia is one of the few spirochetes visible on a routine blood smear, and only while the patient is febrile.
also: Relapsing fever: Borrelia recurrentis (louse) and hermsii (tick)
Antigenic variation of variable surface proteins causes relapses
Lyme disease (B. burgdorferi): serology, not smear
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can follow treatment of spirochetal infections

stem: A 5-year-old boy has been scratching his bottom at night for two weeks, and two classmates have the same complaint. At dawn his mother presses clear adhesive tape against the skin around his anus, and the tape is placed on a slide.
oneliner: 5M + nocturnal perianal itching + classmates affected + tape test of perianal skin → which finding?
ask: Which finding on the tape slide is most likely?

options.B: Thick-shelled eggs with a bumpy outer coat
options.D: Colorless oval eggs flattened on one side

whyNot.A: **Terminal-spine eggs** of S. haematobium are passed in **urine**, not laid on **perianal skin** at night
whyNot.B: **Ascaris** eggs are found in **stool**, and ascariasis does not cause **nocturnal perianal itch**
whyNot.C: **Trichuris** eggs are passed in **stool**, and whipworm causes diarrhea or rectal prolapse, not **night-time perianal itching**
whyNot.E: **S. mansoni** eggs are found in **stool** after freshwater exposure; the tape test samples the **perianal skin**

answer: D-shaped (flattened on one side) eggs of Enterobius vermicularis
why: The female pinworm crawls out at night and lays eggs on the **perianal skin**, causing itch. A **cellophane tape test** in the morning picks up the **eggs flattened on one side**; stool examination is usually negative.

idea.rule: Look for the eggs where the parasite leaves them: Enterobius lays them on perianal skin, so use a tape test, not stool.
also: Enterobius: D-shaped eggs on a morning tape test
Schistosoma haematobium: terminal-spine eggs in urine
Schistosoma mansoni: lateral-spine eggs in stool
Ascaris and Trichuris: eggs in stool

stem: A 24-year-old man has had a single, painless, clean-based firm ulcer on the shaft of his penis for 5 days. He has rubbery, nontender inguinal nodes on both sides. Fluid expressed from the ulcer base is examined unstained under a special microscope.
oneliner: 24M + single painless clean-based indurated penile ulcer + bilateral rubbery nontender inguinal nodes + unstained ulcer fluid → which finding?
ask: Which microscopy finding is most likely?

options.C: Multinucleated giant cells on a scraping

whyNot.A: **H. ducreyi** (chancroid) gives **painful**, soft ulcers with tender suppurative nodes; his ulcer is **painless and firm**
whyNot.C: **HSV** produces **painful vesicles** and ulcers; his lesion is **single, painless and indurated**
whyNot.D: **Gonorrhea** causes purulent urethral discharge, not a **painless indurated ulcer with nontender nodes**
whyNot.E: **Granuloma inguinale** gives a **beefy, bleeding** ulcer without significant lymphadenopathy; he has **bilateral rubbery nodes**

answer: Motile spirochetes on dark-field microscopy (Treponema pallidum)
why: A **painless indurated ulcer with nontender nodes** is a syphilitic chancre. Treponema is **too thin for Gram stain**, so exudate is examined by **dark-field microscopy** (or direct fluorescent antibody) to see **motile corkscrew spirochetes**.

idea.rule: Organisms too thin for light microscopy need dark-field or fluorescence, not a Gram stain.
also: T. pallidum: dark-field microscopy of chancre or condyloma lata
Borrelia: large enough to see on Giemsa blood smear
Leptospira: also seen by dark-field microscopy
Chancroid: painful ulcer, Gram-negative coccobacilli in chains
